final_answer:
No. The trial court most likely did not err (nor abuse its discretion), and mandamus relief to Smith Fullingham should be denied. This fact pattern tracks In re Zaidi (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026, No. 24-0245), which denied mandamus. Caveat: I could not open the full opinion (fetches were blocked); the holdings below come from search-result summaries of Zaidi and Columbia Valley and should be confirmed against the opinion.

1. Framework. Texas courts treat disqualification as a severe remedy, but for side-switching nonlawyer staff apply a bright-line rule from In re American Home Products (Tex. 1998) and In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System (Tex. 2010). (a) It is conclusively presumed that a paralegal/legal assistant who worked on a matter obtained the former client's confidences. Jones qualifies: she prepared litigation documents, took part in several hundred privileged communications, and attended strategy meetings. Her claimed lack of memory does not rebut this irrebuttable presumption. (b) Unlike lawyers, the second presumption, that the nonlawyer shared those confidences with the new firm, is rebuttable, but only if the new firm shows (i) the nonlawyer was instructed not to work on the matter and (ii) the firm took other reasonable measures, at minimum formal, institutionalized screening, to keep her from the file. A merely informal admonition is insufficient. Absent those measures the presumption becomes irrebuttable and the firm is disqualified.

2. Smith Fullingham's measures failed. The firm did not ask about her prior work, gave no admonition, and did no screening when she was hired in 2017 or when she began working on the Apex-Prestige matter (13 occasions of secretarial work and two e-filings). Screening announced only in 2023, after Apex complained, came too late. Per the Zaidi summaries, the Court held that the firm must instruct the nonlawyer, at or before the time she begins work on a conflicted matter, not to work on any matter she worked on in prior employment, regardless of whether she was a side-switcher when hired. Here she was not a side-switcher at hire in the sense the firm knew of the conflict, but the conflict arose in 2017 when the case was remanded, and no admonition was ever given. Her limited, secretarial role and the years elapsed do not matter, because the presumptions do not depend on the extent of her later work.

3. Waiver. A party can waive disqualification by unreasonable delay in complaining (e.g., In re EPIC Holdings, In re Users System Services, not independently verified in this run). Smith Fullingham argued the e-filing notices naming Jones put Apex on notice in 2022. Per the Zaidi summaries, the Court held the notices do not conclusively establish waiver as a matter of law: Apex says it first recognized her name in January 2023, and it moved within about two months (early March 2023). Waiver is a fact-bound issue on which the movant gets deference, so the trial court's implicit rejection of waiver was not an abuse of discretion. Nothing suggests a tactical motive.

Conclusion: because the conclusive first presumption applies, the required instruction and institutional screening were not in place when Jones began working on the matter, and waiver was not established as a matter of law, disqualification was within the trial court's discretion and was not error. Residual uncertainty: the exact reasoning of Zaidi (including any separate writings) and the Dallas court of appeals' own treatment were not verified.

authorities.title: In re Adeel Zaidi, A.K. Chagla and Prestige Consulting d/b/a Turnaround Management Group
authorities.proposition: Firm must instruct nonlawyer at or before beginning work on a conflicted matter, even if not a side-switcher at hire; e-filing notices do not conclusively establish waiver; mandamus denied.

authorities.citation: In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System, L.P., 320 S.W.3d 819 (Tex. 2010)
authorities.title: In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System
authorities.proposition: Conclusive presumption nonlawyer who worked on matter obtained confidences; second presumption rebuttable only by instruction plus formal institutionalized screening; informal admonition insufficient.

claims.text: Texas applies a conclusive presumption that a legal assistant who worked on a matter obtained the client's confidences; lack of recall is irrelevant.

The presumption that the nonlawyer shared confidences with the new firm is rebuttable only by instruction not to work on the matter plus formal institutional screening; absent these it is irrebuttable.
Zaidi requires the admonition at or before the time the nonlawyer starts work on the conflicted matter, regardless of side-switcher status at hire; post-complaint screening comes too late.
E-filing notices naming the nonlawyer do not conclusively establish waiver; prompt motion about two months after discovery supports no waiver as a matter of law.
Therefore the trial court did not err in disqualifying Smith Fullingham.
